vignette:
He is 76 now, a widowed European man who works part-time as a cashier, but when he speaks about himself the years seem to fold back until he is again a younger man trying to survive in a city under bombardment. He describes the war as something that arrived first as a sound: distant explosions, sirens that did not stop, then windows shaking in their frames. At the time, he is living with his wife and two children in a neighborhood that begins to empty out as people leave, are killed, or simply disappear. He remembers the first days of fear as almost ordinary, as if he were waiting for the situation to pass. He still went to work, still stood in line for bread, still tried to behave as though routine could protect them.

The event that changed him most happens during an air raid. He is in the street when the shelling begins, and for a few seconds he cannot make sense of what he hears. Then he sees people running and throws himself down near a wall. Dust and debris fill the air. He loses sight of his wife, who had been a block away carrying groceries, and for several minutes he believes she has been killed. He later finds her crouched in a doorway, shaken but alive. Even after that, he says, something inside him does not settle back into place. The war becomes personal in a different way: every sound is now measured against the possibility of death.

In the months that follow, he learns to live with terror in a state of constant alertness. He scans rooftops, listens for aircraft, watches the faces of strangers for signs of danger. He sleeps lightly, often dressed, with a bag packed by the door. When shelling starts at night, he wakes before anyone else and checks the children’s room. He does not talk much about what he sees—bodies in the street, shattered buildings, neighbors buried under rubble—but the images stay with him. He says they come back most often when the house is quiet, as if silence gives them space to enter. He begins to avoid places that remind him of the war: crowds, loud engines, sudden bangs, news reports. Even now, a car backfiring can make his whole body jerk. His heart races and his hands go cold before he has time to tell himself where he is.

After the war, he and his family rebuild as many people do, in pieces. He survives the loss of friends and the slow erosion of the life he knew. His wife becomes the person who steadies him. She notices that he startles easily, that he is irritable when he is tired, that he sits with his back to the wall in restaurants and watches exits without meaning to. He cannot bear to hear children crying because it pulls him back to the terror of searching for his own children during air raids. He tries to be patient, but he becomes short-tempered, then ashamed of himself. Some nights he wakes from dreams in which he is running through smoke or calling for his wife and cannot find her. He wakes sweating, disoriented, and for a few moments believes the war is still happening.

When his wife dies years later, the ground shifts again beneath him. Her death is not violent, but it strips away the one person who had understood his silences and without whom he feels unmoored. He grieves in a restrained way, as he grieves most things, by staying busy and telling himself he must carry on. Still, he notices that after her death the old memories become sharper. He becomes more watchful, more withdrawn, and less able to distract himself. He goes to work as a cashier because the rhythm helps: greeting customers, scanning items, counting change. The work is simple and predictable, and he likes that there are rules to follow. Yet even there he is not fully at ease. He flinches when a shopping cart crashes into a shelf or when someone raises their voice. He feels foolish about it, but he cannot prevent the surge of fear.

Over time, he has learned that his body remembers what his mind wants to place in the past. He carries the war in the way he pauses at loud noises, in the tiredness that settles over him after a poor night’s sleep, in the way his thoughts drift back to the dead when he is alone. He remains courteous, composed, and proud of being still able to work. But under that steadiness is a constant sense of being braced for something terrible to happen again, as though part of him never left the street where the bombs were falling.
